The Story of Prince Mrigdhvaj

I bow to Lord Jina, worshipped with devotion by the entire world, and I write the story of Prince Mrigdhvaj, as told by the ancient teachers.

Simandhar was king of Ayodhya. His queen was Jinssena. They had a son named Mrigdhvaj. He was deeply addicted to meat — he could not rest a single day without eating it. There was a royal buffalo that would come when called, leave when told, and roll at people's feet. One day the buffalo was playing in a pond. Prince Mrigdhvaj came by with the minister's and merchant's sons. Seeing the buffalo's hooves, some whim seized Mrigdhvaj's mind, and he said to his servant, "Look, today cut off the buffalo's hind leg and cook its meat for me to eat." Saying this, Mrigdhvaj departed. The meat was cooked, and he and his companions ate it with great pleasure.

Meanwhile, the poor buffalo, limping in great pain, fell before the king. The king saw that it was near death. So, without inquiring who had done this, out of compassion he gave it initiation and taught it the Namaskar Mantra. Truly, in this world there are many virtuous, benevolent souls who surpass even the moon, sun, wish-fulfilling tree, and water in their generosity.

The buffalo died and, through the power of the Namaskar Mantra, was reborn as a god in Saudharm heaven. Truly, Lord Jinendra's sacred teaching is genuinely beneficial to living beings.

Afterward, the king investigated who had harmed the buffalo. When he learned it was his own son and the minister's and merchant's sons, his fury knew no bounds. He immediately ordered the minister to have all three killed. The news reached the three young men, and they rushed at once to the monk Munidatt and took Jain initiation. Among them, Mrigdhvaj became a great ascetic. Through intense austerity, he destroyed his destructive karmas through the fire of meditation, attained omniscience, and became worthy of worship by the world. Truly, the power of Jain dharma is so inconceivable that even the greatest sinner, upon embracing it, becomes worthy of worship in all three worlds. And truly, what is superior to dharma?

The monk Mrigdhvaj continued his spiritual practice and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches the transformative power of dharma. Even one who committed a terrible act of cruelty — cutting off a living creature's leg for meat — could, through the grace of initiation and sincere practice, attain the highest spiritual goal. No soul is beyond redemption when it turns toward the path of righteousness.
